blocks.recap_md: The interpreter itself follows a procedure to evaluate a combination: evaluate the subexpressions, then apply the operator's procedure to the operand values.
The evaluation rule is recursive; a deeply nested combination can be pictured as a tree, with values percolating upward from the leaves - an example of tree accumulation.
Primitive expressions are the base case: numerals name numbers, built-in operators name machine instructions, and other names get their value from the environment.
`define` is a special form, not a combination - its whole purpose is to create a name-value association, so it doesn't fit the general evaluate-then-apply rule.

knowledge_items.statement: Evaluating a combination is a recursive process: first evaluate each subexpression (the operator and every operand), then apply the resulting procedure to the resulting argument values.

For primitive expressions, evaluation bottoms out directly: a numeral's value is the number it names, a built-in operator's value is its machine instructions, and any other name's value is whatever it's associated with in the environment.

`define` is a special form, not a combination - it doesn't fit the general evaluate-then-apply rule, since its purpose is precisely to create a new name-value association rather than apply a procedure to already-evaluated arguments.

questions.prompt: According to the evaluation rule given for combinations, what must happen before a procedure can be applied?
options: Every subexpression of the combination (the operator and all operands) must first be evaluated
Only the operands need to be evaluated; the operator is used exactly as written
The whole combination is first converted to a string and parsed a second time
Nothing - application happens first, and evaluation only happens if the result looks incomplete
questions.explanation: The rule is explicitly two steps: evaluate the subexpressions of the combination, then apply the procedure (the value of the leftmost subexpression) to the values of the operands. Evaluation always comes first for every subexpression.

questions.prompt: When the recursive evaluation rule bottoms out at a primitive expression that is a plain name (not a numeral or a built-in operator), what is that name's value?
options: Whatever object is currently associated with that name in the environment
The name's own text, treated as a string
Always 0, since an unbound name has no meaning otherwise
The value of the most recently evaluated combination, regardless of the name
questions.explanation: The text stipulates that the value of a name (other than a built-in operator) is the object associated with that name in the environment - this is exactly why an expression like (+ x 1) is meaningless without an environment that gives x a value.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't `(define x 3)` fit the general evaluate-then-apply rule for combinations?
options: Because define's whole purpose is to associate x with a value, not to apply a procedure to already-evaluated arguments - it's a special form with its own evaluation rule
Because define always signals an error if x already has a value
Because numbers like 3 can never appear as operands in a combination
Because define is actually just an alias for the built-in `+` procedure
questions.explanation: The text is explicit: (define x 3) does not apply define to the value of x and to 3, since the purpose of define is precisely to associate x with a value - that's why define is a special form rather than an ordinary combination, and special forms each get their own evaluation rule.
